description: A proposed modification of the curated Boston Dynamics Spot spec — a what-if build, not fitted hardware: an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano computer and an RPLIDAR A1 2D lidar on a 3D-printed mount post, placed on the body top and powered through Spot's official payload interface — a Boston Dynamics GXP expansion payload on one of the robot's two DB25 payload ports — not from the raw battery rail. The wiring block below is ONLY this payload circuit; the robot's factory harness stays undocumented and is not drawn. The payload circuit is graded in the recorded harness report for this build; the added mass is UNKNOWN — the parts catalog records no mass for any part, and of everything this build adds only the GXP's mass is published (430 g, Boston Dynamics) — so no mass total is stated for the modified robot. Boston Dynamics' published payload limit is 14 kg total, and the photographed unit's arm alone is published at 8 kg against it (SDK Configuration Requirements).
name: Boston Dynamics Spot — Jetson Orin + LiDAR build

wiring.note: PROPOSED payload circuit for the Jetson + LiDAR what-if build — not the robot's factory harness, which is proprietary and undocumented (the base spec carries no wiring block, and none is invented here). Power now comes through Spot's official payload interface, per Boston Dynamics' published documents (retrieved 2026-10-28 and filed in catalog/sources/boston-dynamics-spot.json): a DB25 payload port delivers the unregulated battery bus (35–58.8 V, 150 W per port max, safety interlocks required), and a Spot GXP expansion payload on that port provides regulated rails — 24 V and 12 V sharing 150 W, plus 5 V at a maximum of 10 W — and the RJ45 Ethernet link the Jetson would talk to the robot over. Three verdicts follow from those published figures. (1) The GXP's 5 V rail (10 W = 2 A) cannot run the Jetson at its 15 W or 25 W modes — only the 7 W mode fits it — so the Jetson is fed from the 24 V rail through the catalog's 5 V buck, whose 24 V maximum input the regulated rail respects exactly, with no margin. (An earlier draft of this build fed that buck from the raw pack rail at 50.4 V and the viewer flagged it red; that topology is retired, not hidden — the change is recorded in the retrieval plan.) (2) The lidar rides the GXP's 5 V rail, which it shares with nothing else in this build; its draw is unrecorded, so that rail grades PARTIAL. (3) The direct-port alternative — a wide-input regulator on the unregulated bus, with components Boston Dynamics says should handle at least 80 V input — cannot be graded here: the parts catalog stocks no such regulator. Cable gauges and lengths on payload-side runs are design choices for the proposed build, labelled proposed in the connection labels; the port-to-GXP ribbon cable's 225 mm is the published length of the cable supplied with the GXP. Currents are stated only where published or catalog numbers derive them.
